papers.title: Less is More: Unbiased Galaxy Clustering from Fewer Merger Trees
papers.authors: Oscar J. Hickman, Sownak Bose, Kai Wang, Carlton M. Baugh, Baojiu Li
papers.abstract: Galaxy clustering could strongly constrain galaxy formation models but is rarely used, because the two-point correlation function (2PCF) requires a complete galaxy catalogue at every point in parameter space. Semi-analytic models (SAMs) process each halo merger tree independently, so running a SAM on $m$ of $k$ disjoint partitions of the trees, each spanning the full box, cuts the cost by $k/m$. Because a halo's galaxies are kept or discarded together, one-halo pairs are diluted less than two-halo pairs, and the naive estimate overstates small-scale clustering by a factor $k/m$. We introduce the Sparse and Unbiased Clustering Estimator (SaUCE), which removes this bias with weights set by $m$ and $k$ alone. It has no free parameters, gives exactly unbiased pair counts, and applies to any catalogue built from a random subset of whole haloes and to any pair-count statistic. Running a SAM on 7 per cent of the P-Millennium merger trees, 68 per cent of random selections recover the full-box $\xi(r)$ at $z=0$ to within 0.05 dex in each bin from 0.03 to $30\,h^{-1}\,\mathrm{Mpc}$, at a density of $10^{-2}\,h^{3}\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-3}$: a fourteen-fold computational saving. The required fraction rises with redshift and as the number density falls, is the same for two model variants, and transfers between boxes through the galaxy and pair counts. The scatter, derived in closed form, is strongly correlated between bins, so a likelihood must use the full covariance. A recipe for choosing the fraction makes the 2PCF affordable for model calibration and simulation-based inference.

conclusions: Naively running a SAM on a random fraction $m/k$ of merger trees overestimates small-scale clustering by a factor of $k/m$ (up to $\sim 128\times$ in their tests) because intra-halo galaxy pairs are diluted linearly ($m/k$) while inter-halo pairs are diluted quadratically ($\sim (m/k)^2$).

The proposed SaUCE estimator applies exact Horvitz–Thompson inverse-probability weights—$w_{\rm auto} = m/k$ for same-partition pairs and $w_{\rm cross} = m(k-1)/[k(m-1)]$ for cross-partition pairs—with zero free parameters, yielding an unbiased two-point correlation function across real space, redshift-space multipoles, and projected statistics.

At $z=0$ and a galaxy number density of $\bar{n} = 10^{-2}\,h^3\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-3}$ in the P-Millennium simulation, running GALFORM on just $7.3\%$ of merger trees recovers the full-box $\xi(r)$ within $0.05\,\mathrm{dex}$ ($12\%$) across $0.03 < r < 30\,h^{-1}\,\mathrm{Mpc}$ ($14\times$ speedup).

The required partition fraction increases at higher redshifts and lower number densities (reaching $29\%$ at $z \approx 1.5$, $\bar{n} = 10^{-3}\,h^3\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-3}$, and $96\%$ at $\bar{n} = 10^{-4}\,h^3\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-3}$), and because subsample errors are strongly correlated across radial bins, parameter inference requires using the full bin-to-bin covariance matrix.

ai.summary: Calibrating semi-analytic models (SAMs)—which populate dark matter halo merger trees from $N$-body simulations with galaxies using simplified baryonic physics prescriptions—against observed galaxy clustering is normally too computationally expensive for MCMC or simulation-based inference, because evaluating the two-point correlation function ($\xi(r)$) at each parameter point requires processing millions of merger trees across an entire simulation box. While one can cut runtime by running the SAM on only a random subset ($m$ out of $k$ partitions) of whole merger trees scattered across the box, doing so naively biases small-scale clustering upwards by a factor of $k/m$: galaxies within the same halo (one-halo pairs) are always kept or discarded together with probability $m/k$, whereas pairs in different haloes (two-halo pairs) require both host trees to be selected with probability $\sim (m/k)^2$. The authors introduce the Sparse and Unbiased Clustering Estimator (SaUCE), which eliminates this bias exactly without free parameters by separately weighting galaxy pairs within the same tree partition and across different partitions by their exact inverse selection probabilities. Validating SaUCE with the GALFORM SAM on the P-Millennium and Millennium simulations, they show it recovers accurate real- and redshift-space clustering at a fraction of the computational cost, making full two-point clustering viable for SAM calibration and simulation-based inference.

papers.title: Fast Scrambling Cosmology
papers.authors: Aliv Sahoo, Fatima Abbasi, Jake McNaughton, Niayesh Afshordi
papers.abstract: Quantum gravity arguments such as trans-Planckian censorship suggest that de Sitter space can only last for a time of order $H^{-1}\ln(M_{\rm Pl}/H)$, corresponding to the fast-scrambling time of black hole and cosmological horizons. We ask whether this clock leaves an imprint on cosmic expansion, via a minimal modification of the Raychaudhuri equation that adds a term $-\Gamma H^2/\ln(M_{\rm Pl}^2/H^2)$ to $\dot H$, with $\Gamma={\cal O}(1)$. The slowly varying $\sigma\equiv\Gamma/\ln(M_{\rm Pl}^2/H^2)\ll 1$ is nearly constant at late times. De Sitter space is replaced by a slowly evolving vacuum (an exact Lambert-$W$ solution), and for constant $\sigma$ the expansion rate is found in closed form for arbitrary matter sources. The correction acts as dark energy with two components: a vacuum mode with $w=-1+2\sigma/3$, and a term that integrates over the history of the cosmic fluids, so that any change in the equation of state of a species leaves a permanent residual; e.g., neutrinos becoming non-relativistic shift the dark energy density by ${\cal O}(\sigma m_\nu^4)$. A covariant clock-field completion reproduces this background, and a term that rescales the gravitational constant governing cosmic expansion removes its short-wavelength instability in the dark-energy era. Big Bang nucleosynthesis constraints give a proxy bound $\Gamma=-3.7\pm6.1$ (68% confidence), while the negative-$\Gamma$ branch qualitatively follows the $w_0w_a$CDM dark energy evolution inferred from DESI DR2 at $z\gtrsim1$. The early-time tracking terms amount to a similar rescaling, for which existing fits to cosmic microwave background (CMB), baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) and supernova data translate into the proxy estimate $\Gamma\simeq-2.8\pm0.9$ ($\sigma\simeq-0.01$ today). These background-level results motivate a dedicated likelihood analysis of structure formation in this theory.

conclusions: In the nearly constant $\sigma \equiv \Gamma/\ln(M_{\rm Pl}^2/H^2) \ll 1$ regime, the modified Raychaudhuri equation decomposes into an effective dark energy vacuum mode with equation of state $w_{\rm vac} = -1 + 2\sigma/3$ and tracking terms that rescale the effective gravitational coupling $G_{\rm eff}/G_{\rm N}$ during radiation and matter domination.

Mapping these early-time tracking terms onto existing "cosmic glitch in gravity" fits (combining Planck/ACT/SPT CMB, DESI DR2 BAO, and DES SNe) yields a proxy estimate of $\Gamma \simeq -2.8 \pm 0.9$ ($\sigma \simeq -0.0110 \pm 0.0033$, a $\sim 3\sigma$ preference for negative $\Gamma$), while BBN light-element bounds give $\Gamma = -3.7 \pm 6.1$ (68% CL).

For $\Gamma < 0$ ($\sigma < 0$), the effective vacuum energy is mildly phantom-like and its background evolution qualitatively tracks the $w_0w_a$CDM trajectory inferred from DESI DR2 at $z \gtrsim 1$, ultimately driving $H$ toward the Planck scale over $\sim 100\,H_0^{-1} \simeq 1.4\text{ Tyr}$.

Because the effective dark energy includes an integral over the source history, any change in the equation of state of cosmic species leaves a permanent residual; for example, massive neutrinos becoming non-relativistic shift the late-time dark energy density by $\mathcal{O}(\sigma m_\nu^4)$.

A minimal covariant scalar-clock completion of this background suffers from a sub-horizon gradient instability ($c_s^2 < 0$ at all epochs), though adding a Hořava–Lifshitz/cuscuton-type $\Theta^2$ operator regulates short-wavelength instabilities in the dark-energy era.

The authors explore whether this horizon clock leaves an observable imprint on cosmic expansion by adding a phenomenological decay/growth term $-\Gamma H^2/\ln(M_{\rm Pl}^2/H^2) \equiv -\sigma H^2$ to the background Raychaudhuri equation for $\dot{H}$. Solving the modified expansion history analytically in the slowly varying $\sigma$ limit, they show that this term acts as an effective dynamical dark energy with two pieces: a slowly evolving vacuum mode and a "memory" integral over the cosmic fluid history that rescales the effective gravitational constant $G_{\rm cosmo}$ in each era. They also construct a covariant scalar-field "clock" action to reproduce this background and obtain preliminary proxy constraints on $\Gamma$ by mapping the fluid-tracking terms onto existing BBN and CMB+DESI BAO+SNe analyses, motivating future perturbation and structure-formation studies.

papers.title: Millimeter-Wavelength Constraints on Circular Polarization of the Cosmic Microwave Background at Arcminute Scales with the Simons Array
papers.authors: POLARBEAR Collaboration : Kam Arnold, Darcy R. Barron, Matthew R. Chu, Nicole Farias, Takuro Fujino, Masaya Hasegawa, Haruaki Hirose, Kailey Hwang, Ethan H. Ish, Jennifer Ito, Brian Keating, Adrian T. Lee, Anto I. Lonappan, Alec Miyashita, Lindsay Ng Lowry, Luke M. Porter, Shahed Shayan Arani, Praween Siritanasak
papers.abstract: We present constraints on the cosmic microwave background (CMB) circular polarization anisotropy at arcminute angular scales, using dedicated measurements from the Simons Array taken with a quarter-wave plate and rotating half-wave plate. A detection of circular polarization in the CMB would probe a range of proposed generation mechanisms, from Standard Model astrophysics to physics beyond it. At an observing frequency of 90 GHz, we place constraints over the multipole range $300 \leq \ell \leq 2000$, corresponding to angular scales of 5.4-36 arcmin, in bands of width $\Delta \ell = 100$, roughly tripling the highest multipole previously reached by a $V$-mode power spectrum measurement. Within this domain, we constrain the 95% confidence upper bound of $\ell (\ell+1) C_\ell^{VV} / (2\pi)$ to range from ${\sim}22\,\mu\mathrm{K}_\mathrm{CMB}^2$ at the $\ell = 350$ bandpower to ${\sim}3.5\times10^3\,\mu\mathrm{K}_\mathrm{CMB}^2$ at the $\ell = 1950$ bandpower. These limits are derived from ${\sim}2.5$ months of observations of each of two small regions of the sky located away from the Galactic plane, totaling ${\sim}12\,\mathrm{deg}^2$ of effective sky area. Because the methodology of this study marginalizes known foreground contamination, these bounds serve as robust, conservative limits on the true CMB circular polarization signal down to the sensitivity limits of the instrument. Additionally, we provide an experimental and analytical framework for implementing circular polarization observations on other telescopes by utilizing a quarter-wave plate and half-wave plate design.

conclusions: At $90\text{ GHz}$ over the multipole range $300 \leq \ell \leq 2000$ (angular scales of $5.4\text{--}36\text{ arcmin}$), the 95% confidence upper limits on the circular polarization power spectrum $\ell(\ell+1)C_\ell^{VV}/(2\pi)$ span from $\sim 22\,\mu\mathrm{K}_\mathrm{CMB}^2$ at $\ell = 350$ to $\sim 3.5 \times 10^3\,\mu\mathrm{K}_\mathrm{CMB}^2$ at $\ell = 1950$, set primarily by the instrumental noise floor.

These measurements extend $V$-mode power spectrum constraints to multipoles roughly three times higher than previous studies (providing the only $V$-mode bandpower bounds above $\ell \approx 700$ to date) and improve upon prior $95\text{ GHz}$ SPIDER limits by a factor of a few in their overlapping multipole bin.

The combined quarter-wave and half-wave plate optical system achieves a laboratory circular-to-linear conversion efficiency of $99.0\%$ and a net on-sky circular polarization efficiency of $\eta_V = 0.528 \pm 0.032$, demonstrating a viable experimental framework for repurposing linear-polarization CMB receivers to measure Stokes $V$.

Current $90\text{ GHz}$ upper limits remain roughly six orders of magnitude in power above theoretical predictions for secondary CMB circular polarization; because Faraday conversion scales with frequency as $\nu^{-3}$, future experiments observing at lower frequencies ($\sim 10\text{ GHz}$) or leveraging massive detector arrays like the Simons Observatory will be required to close this sensitivity gap.
ai.summary: In standard $\Lambda$CDM cosmology, the cosmic microwave background (CMB) exhibits linear polarization ($E$ and $B$ modes) from Thomson scattering at recombination, but virtually zero circular polarization (Stokes $V$ modes, where the electric field vector rotates in a circle). However, a small circular polarization signal could be generated by secondary effects—such as Faraday conversion as CMB photons pass through magnetized relativistic plasmas in galaxy clusters or Population III supernova remnants—or by beyond-Standard-Model physics like primordial magnetic fields and axion-like pseudoscalar fields. In this paper, the POLARBEAR Collaboration places the first arcminute-scale ($300 \leq \ell \leq 2000$) constraints on CMB circular polarization at $90\text{ GHz}$ using five months of data across $\sim 12\text{ deg}^2$ of sky from the Polarbear-2b receiver on the Simons Array. To measure circular polarization with detectors built for linear polarization, they placed a stationary grooved-plastic quarter-wave plate in front of their continuously rotating cryogenic half-wave plate, converting incoming Stokes $V$ signals into linear Stokes $U$ polarization that is cleanly modulated away from low-frequency atmospheric noise. While the resulting upper limits are still orders of magnitude above theoretical expectations due to elevated instrument noise, this work triples the maximum multipole $\ell$ ever probed in $V$ modes and establishes a practical optical and analytical blueprint for measuring circular polarization with existing CMB telescopes.

papers.title: OASIS: A Fast Dynamical Halo Finding Algorithm
papers.authors: Bayli Hayes, Edgar M. Salazar, Eduardo Rozo, Benedikt Diemer, Calvin Osinga, John Hugon, Vadim Bernshteyn, Ze'ev Vladimir
papers.abstract: In recent work (García et al. 2023), we advocated for defining a dynamical halo as the collection of particles that orbit their self-generated potential. Here we introduce the Orbiting-mass ASsIgnment Scheme (OASIS), a fast energy-based algorithm for constructing dynamical halo catalogs. Using single-snapshot information, OASIS achieves $\simeq 9\%$ scatter in orbiting mass estimates relative to the SPARTA particle-tracking algorithm. As an illustration of the applications enabled by OASIS, we use the Quijote and Erebos simulation suites to show that the $z=0$ dynamical halo mass function is nearly universal with respect to cosmology, and that it is well described by a modified Press-Schechter form with an effective collapse threshold $\delta_{\rm sc} = 1.54$ at intermediate masses. However, this description fails at high masses.

conclusions: **Fast single-snapshot dynamical halo finding**: OASIS identifies orbiting halo mass from a single simulation snapshot by applying an energy-based threshold in kinetic energy versus radius, recovering orbiting masses from expensive multi-snapshot tracking codes (SPARTA) with only $\simeq 9\%$ scatter and processing a $1024^3$ box in $\sim 10$ minutes on 16 cores.

**Universal kinetic energy boundary**: The energy-space boundary separating virialized orbiting particles from infalling particles is mass-independent and depends on cosmology and redshift solely through a logarithmic scaling with $\Omega_{\rm m}(z)$, making the selection rule universal once scaled by virial units ($R_{\rm 200b}$, $v_{\rm 200b}$).

**Dynamical halo mass function universality**: Evaluated across 100 Quijote Latin hypercube cosmologies, the $z=0$ dynamical halo mass function is universal with respect to cosmological parameters to within $\approx 5\%$, consistent with expected $2\text{--}4\%$ systematic uncertainties in dynamical mass assignment.

**Modified Press-Schechter collapse threshold**: Intermediate-mass dynamical halo abundances are well fit by a modified Press-Schechter formalisation with an effective spherical collapse threshold $\delta_{\rm sc} = 1.54$ (with $1.4\%$ scatter), though this description breaks down at the highest mass scales and fails to capture the low-mass slope without modifications.

ai.summary: Standard halo definitions based on spherical overdensities or splashback radii inevitably blend dynamically bound, orbiting particles with newly infalling matter crossing the boundary for the first time. Accurately disentangling these two populations usually requires tracing particle trajectories across multiple simulation snapshots using codes like SPARTA, which is computationally expensive for large cosmological simulation suites. To solve this, Hayes et al. introduce OASIS (Orbiting-mass ASsIgnment Scheme), a fast algorithm that post-processes single-snapshot halo seeds (from Rockstar) by separating orbiting from infalling particles using a calibrated linear cut in log kinetic energy versus radius, augmented by a core correction and substructure assignment. Tested across the Quijote and Erebos simulation suites, OASIS recovers dynamical halo masses with $\simeq 9\%$ scatter relative to particle-tracking methods, runs in $\approx 10$ minutes per box, and enables efficient population-level studies such as testing the cosmological universality of the dynamical halo mass function.

papers.title: The unified bound dark energy--bound dark matter model confronted with DESI DR2, ACT and SPT-3G, and the Unite supernovae measurements
papers.authors: Jose Agustin Lozano Torres, Axel de la Macorra
papers.abstract: The unified bound dark energy-bound dark matter (BDE-BDM) model derives the whole dark sector from a single supersymmetric SU(3) dark gauge group, whose lightest meson is the dark energy and whose heavier bound states, created with a velocity $v_c$ when the group condenses, are the dark matter. Because the condensation scale $\Lambda_c$ is fixed by gauge-coupling unification, the dark-energy sector has no free parameter beyond those of $\Lambda$CDM, and the dark-matter sector adds only $v_c$. We confront the model with DESI DR2 baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO), the Planck, ACT DR6 and SPT-3G D1 CMB spectra, the combined ACT and SPT CMB lensing and the Unite supernovae. The measured condensation scale, $\Lambda_c=43.74\pm0.11$ eV, lies inside the window $34^{+16}_{-11}$ eV predicted by unification, and the dark energy thaws without ever crossing the phantom divide, reaching $w_0=-0.9267\pm0.0003$ today; it thus reproduces the DESI distances that $w_0w_a$CDM fits with a phantom past. BDE-BDM gives the best fit to the DESI DR2 BAO of the four models, reducing $\chi^2_{\rm BAO}$ by 20% with respect to $\Lambda$CDM, more than $w_0w_a$CDM, and over the full data combination it is statistically equivalent to both $\Lambda$CDM and $w_0w_a$CDM, with $\ln B=-0.50$ and $-0.15$, while having two fewer dark-energy parameters than $w_0w_a$CDM. Within bound dark energy, bound dark matter is moderately preferred over cold dark matter, $\ln B=+3.2$ with $\Delta\chi^2=-9.0$, mostly from the CMB. The data now constrain the bound velocity from both sides, $v_c=0.37\pm0.14$, which places the free-streaming cutoff of the matter power spectrum at $k_{1/2}=1.49\,h$ Mpc$^{-1}$ and lowers the amplitude of structure to $S_8=0.807\pm0.007$. Future high-redshift and Lyman-$\alpha$ forest data, together with growth and lensing measurements, will therefore provide the decisive tests of the unified dark sector.

conclusions: Excellent fit to DESI without phantom crossing: The model reduces χ²_BAO for DESI DR2 by 20% compared to ΛCDM (fitting BAO better than w0waCDM) via a purely thawing equation of state (w0 = -0.9267 ± 0.0003, wa = -0.847 ± 0.004) that stays strictly non-phantom throughout cosmic history.

Physical condensation scale confirmed: The fitted condensation scale Λc = 43.74 ± 0.11 eV matches the theoretical SUSY gauge coupling unification prediction (34^+16_-11 eV), with 94% of the condensation energy funnelled into dark energy (f_BDE = 0.9398 ± 0.0037) and 6% into dark matter.

Bound dark matter velocity detected: Small-scale CMB and lensing data constrain the dark matter emergence velocity to vc = 0.37 ± 0.14 (0.066 < vc < 0.60 at 95% CL), ruling out standard cold dark matter (vc -> 0) within this unified framework at 95% CL and yielding a Bayesian preference of ln B = +3.2 over BDE+CDM.

Suppression of small-scale structure (S8): Free-streaming of the bound dark matter imposes a matter power spectrum cutoff at k_{1/2} = 1.49 h/Mpc, lowering the structure amplitude to S8 = 0.807 ± 0.007 (σ8 = 0.795 ± 0.005) and predicting a lower growth rate fσ8 at DESI redshifts compared to ΛCDM.

Hubble tension remains unchanged: Because the dark energy density is negligible around recombination and leaves the sound horizon unaffected (rd = 147.50 ± 0.17 Mpc), the inferred Hubble constant from BAO+CMB remains low at H0 = 67.22 ± 0.22 km/s/Mpc (5.5σ below SH0ES).

The authors test an alternative, unified dark sector model where dark energy and dark matter originate from a single supersymmetric SU(3) gauge group that undergoes confinement (condensation) at an energy scale Λc ~ 40 eV, producing a light scalar meson that drives late-time cosmic acceleration (bound dark energy) and heavier bound states that act as dark matter with an initial formation velocity vc (bound dark matter). Confronting this model with DESI DR2 BAO, high-resolution CMB data (Planck, ACT DR6, SPT-3G), CMB lensing, and the Unite supernova compilation, they find it reproduces the DESI expansion history through physical "thawing" (w >= -1) rather than a phantom past, all while having no extra free dark energy parameters once Λc is specified by gauge unification. Furthermore, the free-streaming of the relativistic bound dark matter naturally suppresses small-scale clustering, easing the S8 tension.

papers.title: Scalar-Induced Gravitational Waves Probing Phase Transitions in the Standard Model and Beyond
papers.authors: Peizhi Du, Xiang-Xi Zeng, Jiahang Zhong
papers.abstract: Scalar-induced gravitational waves (SIGWs) are unique messengers of physics in the early Universe and possible sources for the observed data from pulsar timing arrays (PTAs). It has been demonstrated that SIGWs have the potential to probe cosmological phase transitions via measurement of the equation of state and sound speed of the cosmic thermal bath, which have non-trivial time dependence during phase transitions. In this work, we improve on existing studies of SIGWs in a time-dependent background with time-dependent initial conditions and an entropy-conserving thermal history of the Standard Model (SM). We provide possible physical explanations for features of the gravitational wave spectrum from phase transitions, the most prominent of which for a scale-invariant curvature spectrum is a step due to entropy dilution. We show that current and future gravitational wave observations across a wide range of frequencies can probe phase transitions in the SM and physics beyond the Standard Model (BSM). Signals from the QCD crossover appear around 10 nHz, inside the observable window of PTAs. We perform data analyses using NANOGrav 15-year data, showing a mild preference for the QCD crossover over standard radiation domination for two choices of curvature spectra. BSM phase transitions in the TeV range lead to signals around mHz, which are accessible in future space-based experiments such as LISA, Taiji and TianQin.

conclusions: Entropy-conserving background and exact initial conditions: By constructing a thermodynamically consistent equation of state $w(T)$ and sound speed $c_s^2(T)$ from lattice QCD data and deriving exact superhorizon initial conditions for metric perturbations, the authors resolve entropy non-conservation issues and remove spurious spectral peaks present in earlier literature.

Characteristic spectral features: Phase transitions imprint identifiable features on the induced tensor spectrum, primarily an overall step-like suppression driven by entropy dilution ($R \propto g_{*s}^{-1/3}$), along with an infrared peak and an ultraviolet dip near the transition scale.

Mild preference in NANOGrav 15-year data: Bayesian parameter inference with NANOGrav 15-year PTA data shows a very mild statistical preference for the QCD crossover thermal history over pure radiation domination (Bayes factor $\mathcal{B}_{\rm QCD/RD} = 1.36$ for a broken power-law curvature spectrum) and alters the best-fit scale for delta-function spectra.

Multi-band observational prospects: The QCD crossover falls squarely in the nanohertz band accessible to pulsar timing arrays, whereas electroweak and TeV-scale beyond-the-Standard-Model transitions (e.g. composite Higgs models) generate signals in the $\mu\mathrm{Hz}$ to $\mathrm{mHz}$ range targetable by future space-based interferometers like LISA, Taiji, and TianQin.

ai.summary: In the early universe, primordial scalar curvature perturbations generate tensor modes at second order, producing scalar-induced gravitational waves (SIGWs) that carry pristine records of early cosmic thermodynamics. Standard SIGW calculations assume idealized radiation domination with a constant equation of state ($w=1/3$) and sound speed ($c_s^2=1/3$), but during cosmic phase transitions—such as the QCD or electroweak crossovers—the changing relativistic degrees of freedom cause both parameters to drop and alter cosmic expansion. In this paper, the authors resolve two shortcomings in prior work by deriving exact superhorizon initial conditions for metric perturbations in time-dependent backgrounds and constructing an explicitly entropy-conserving thermal history from lattice QCD data. They compute the corrected SIGW spectrum across Standard Model and TeV-scale beyond-the-Standard-Model transitions, showing that features such as entropy dilution steps naturally emerge and testing the predictions against NANOGrav 15-year pulsar timing array data. This provides a rigorous, thermodynamically consistent pipeline to translate stochastic gravitational wave measurements across nanohertz to millihertz frequencies into constraints on high-energy phase transitions.

papers.title: Self-Interacting Neutrinos in NEDE and DRMD Cosmologies: Posteriors, profiles and evidence using CLiENT
papers.authors: Magnus Uggerhøj, Tobias Johannessen, Jeppe Pagaard Thybo, Steen Hannestad, Thomas Tram
papers.abstract:
A large number of extensions of the $\Lambda$CDM model have been proposed as solutions to the Hubble tension, but they are almost always tested separately. Combinations of such models are rarely studied, and one reason is that their parameter spaces are very costly to explore with standard methods. Here we study a combination of two models which have each been proposed as a solution: self-interacting neutrinos (SI$
u$) and the dark radiation matter decoupling (DRMD) of hot new early dark energy. The SI$
u$+DRMD model has twelve cosmological parameters, a bimodal posterior in the neutrino self-interaction and several flat directions in parameter space, and it can only be investigated in detail because we use the likelihood emulator CLiENT. With emulators trained on about $3	imes 10^5$ likelihood evaluations per dataset we obtain posteriors, best fits and profile likelihoods for the model and for the models nested within it, and all quoted $\chi^2$ values are calculated with the true likelihood. We use two data combinations, both with and without the SH0ES calibration: a conservative one consisting of Planck, DESI BAO and Pantheon+ supernovae, and a more aggressive one in which the small-scale CMB spectra come from ACT and SPT. With the most aggressive combination, the SI$
u$+DRMD model provides a much better fit than either SI$
u$ or DRMD on its own, and its posterior gives $H_0 = 70.94\pm 0.60$ km/s/Mpc. It lowers the $\chi^2$ of $\Lambda$CDM by 27.6, compared with 9.9 for DRMD and 4.0 for SI$
u$, i.e. by more than the sum of the two ($\Delta$AIC = -15.7 relative to DRMD, in terms of the Akaike information criterion). This shows that combined models can fit the data considerably better than the individual models, and it demonstrates the value of being able to analyse such complex models in detail.

conclusions: **Synergistic tension relief:** When fitted to small-scale CMB data (ACT and SPT) alongside Planck, DESI BAO, Pantheon+, and SH0ES, the combined $\text{SI}\nu+\text{DRMD}$ model yields $H_0 = 70.94 \pm 0.60\text{ km s}^{-1}\text{ Mpc}^{-1}$ and improves the fit over $\Lambda$CDM by $\Delta\chi^2 = -27.6$ (more than the sum of $-9.9$ from DRMD and $-4.0$ from $\text{SI}\nu$ alone), strongly favouring the combination with $\Delta\text{AIC} = -15.7$ relative to DRMD.

**Physical mechanism of complementarity:** At intermediate coupling strengths, self-interacting neutrinos delay free-streaming and alter acoustic driving, allowing for higher dark radiation density ($\Delta N_\mathrm{eff}$) and a higher $H_0$ without requiring the anomalously high primordial spectral index ($n_s$) that DRMD alone needs to match the CMB damping tail.

**Dataset sensitivity:** For conservative data (Planck + DESI + Pantheon+) or when excluding the SH0ES prior, the additional parameter complexity is not justified by the AIC, showing that the preference for combined models is driven by the local distance ladder tension and small-scale CMB.

**Strongly interacting neutrino mode suppressed:** High-multipole ACT and SPT data suppress the strongly interacting neutrino mode ($\log_{10}(G_\mathrm{eff}\,\text{MeV}^2) \sim -1.7$) that was present in Planck-only analyses, favouring intermediate or moderate interaction strengths.

**Feasibility via likelihood emulation:** Using CLiENT (active-learning neural network likelihood emulation) achieved sub-unit log-likelihood RMS precision ($0.09\text{--}0.37$), making an otherwise intractable 12-cosmological-parameter nested sampling run (~76 core-years of exact Boltzmann evaluations) computationally practical.

ai.summary: Early-universe solutions to the Hubble tension—such as self-interacting neutrinos ($\text{SI}\nu$), which delay free-streaming and suppress anisotropic stress, or Dark Radiation Matter Decoupling (DRMD) from hot New Early Dark Energy, which alters early expansion and perturbation growth—are almost always analyzed in isolation because exploring combined high-dimensional parameter spaces is computationally prohibitive. papers.abstract: Cosmic string networks are predicted in some early-Universe scenarios, and in certain models, the string tension becomes a function of time. papers.title: Connecting field-level and n-point function measurements of galaxy bias
papers.authors: Hsiang-Ming Huang, Henrique Rubira, Fabian Schmidt
papers.abstract: Precise measurements of galaxy bias parameters are essential for extracting cosmological information from galaxy surveys. Field-level analyses infer bias coefficients at a finite cutoff $\Lambda$, typically related to the lattice resolution, while $n$-point function analyses typically adopt renormalization conditions defined in the low-$k$ limit. We show that the RG predictions describe the measured running and, in the limit $\Lambda\to 0$, agree with the (tree-level) $n$-point function measurements of first-order $b_\delta$ and second-order $b_{\delta^2}, b_{{G}_2}$. We also measure the running on halo catalogs based on full $N$-body simulations and show that the RG prediction describes the measurements well within the predicted systematic errors. Our results establish the RG flow as a natural formulation for relating galaxy bias measurements at different cutoffs and connecting the schemes used in field-level and $n$-point function analyses.

A dedicated spectral analysis demonstrates that none of the candidates shows a statistically significant preference for dark matter annihilation over standard astrophysical emitters. By comparing the surviving candidates to subhalo abundances predicted by repopulated Milky Way N-body simulations, they place upper bounds on the WIMP annihilation cross section $\langle\sigma v\rangle$, demonstrating that unassociated catalog sources provide a valuable, independent complement to dwarf galaxy searches.

papers.title: TITAN DR1: The Type Ia Supernova Trove from ATLAS in the Nearby Universe - Host Galaxies I: Associations, Redshifts and Derived Properties
papers.authors: Jack W. Tweddle, Yukei S. Murakami, Maria Vincenzi, Stephen J. Smartt, Bastien Carreres, Fiorenzo Stoppa, Erik R. Peterson, Brodie Popovic, Jasper Milstein, MaKenzie Elliott, Elijah G. Marlin, Dillon Brout, David O. Jones, Mitchell Dixon, Adam G. Riess, Daniel M. Scolnic, Alejandro Clocchiatti
papers.abstract: We present the host-galaxy catalogue for TITAN DR1, a sample of 8378 spectroscopically confirmed Type Ia supernovae (SNe~Ia) at $z \lesssim 0.15$ -- the largest homogeneous low-redshift SN Ia sample assembled to date. We describe the association of each SN with its host, the compilation of redshifts, measurements of uniform far-ultraviolet to mid-infrared (FUV--MIR) photometry, and the derivation of host properties through spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting. Combining four host-association methods with manual vetting, we securely identify hosts for 7856 SNe~Ia (93.8\%). We compile host-galaxy spectroscopic redshifts for 5522 objects and provide CMB-frame and peculiar-velocity-corrected redshifts. \rev{PSF-matched} photometry is measured for 7568 host galaxies, including both global fluxes and local optical-only fluxes within a fixed 1.5~kpc aperture centred on the SN; \texttt{Bagpipes} returns successful global fits for \rev{all} hosts and local fits for 7329. Stellar mass and rest-frame $g-z$ colour are robustly measured from optical data alone, whereas reliable estimates of star-formation rate, dust attenuation, and mass-weighted age require broader wavelength coverage to break age--dust degeneracies\rev{, and are reported for 5827 hosts}; in our redshift range, MIR data suffice and far-IR coverage is not required. The hosts span a representative low-redshift galaxy population, with a median stellar mass of $\log_{10}(M_*/M_\odot)=10.22$ (\rev{60\%} high-mass; $\log_{10}(M_*/M_\odot)>10$), \rev{71\%} star-forming ($\log_{10}(\mathrm{sSFR}/\mathrm{yr}^{-1}) > -10.5$), and an approximately exponential $A_V$ distribution. This catalogue provides the foundation for forthcoming analyses of the luminosity step and the broader role of galaxy environment in SN~Ia standardization and cosmology.

**Robust SED fitting without far-IR:** Demonstrated that optical photometry reliably recovers stellar mass, while mid-IR (WISE) data successfully break age–dust degeneracies to yield robust star-formation rates, ages, and dust attenuation ($A_V$) for 5,827 hosts without requiring scarce far-infrared data.

**Host demographics:** The host galaxies represent a typical low-redshift population with a median stellar mass of $\log_{10}(M_*/M_\odot) = 10.22$ (60% massive hosts with $M_* > 10^{10} M_\odot$), 71% star-forming ($\log_{10}(\mathrm{sSFR}/\mathrm{yr}^{-1}) > -10.5$), and an approximately exponential $A_V$ distribution.

**Cosmological impact:** Delivers the largest homogeneous low-redshift ($z \lesssim 0.15$) host sample to date, establishing an empirical baseline to determine whether SN Ia luminosity step corrections are driven by host mass, stellar age, or dust.

Using a combination of four automated matching algorithms and visual inspection, they identify host galaxies, compile host spectroscopic redshifts with peculiar-velocity corrections, and perform multi-wavelength spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting from the far-UV to the mid-IR. They show that mid-infrared data from WISE are sufficient to break age–dust degeneracies in nearby galaxies without requiring scarce far-infrared observations. This work establishes the largest homogeneous low-redshift SN Ia host sample to date, providing the essential empirical benchmark for calibrating environmental systematics in Stage-IV cosmological analyses.

papers.title: Helicity Decay to Baryons: The Cosmological Evolution of $L_μ-L_τ$ Gauge Fields and Baryogenesis
papers.authors: Kohei Kamada, Fumio Uchida, Di Wu
papers.abstract: We study baryogenesis from the post-inflationary decay of helical U(1)$_{L_\mu-L_\tau}$ gauge fields generated during axion inflation. Assuming that Schwinger pair production is suppressed during inflation, a large helicity-to-entropy ratio $\eta_H$ can be generated while keeping the initial lepton asymmetry just after inflation negligible. After reheating, the dissipation of magnetic helicity sources a lepton asymmetry through the chiral anomaly, which is partially converted into a baryon asymmetry by electroweak sphaleron processes. We find that there are parameter spaces where the observed baryon asymmetry can be generated in both the turbulent and dissipation-dominated regimes of the U(1)$_{L_\mu-L_\tau}$ magnetic field evolution. The baryon asymmetry generation in the turbulent regime is, however, dominated by the pre-turbulent nearly frozen regime. We further find that the requirement of successful baryogenesis imposes stronger constraints on the inflationary Hubble parameter and the helicity density generated during axion inflation than the requirement for the gauge-field energy not to backreact on the inflaton dynamics.

conclusions: **Baryogenesis via early helicity dissipation**: Dissipation of helical $U(1)_{L_\mu - L_\tau}$ magnetic fields before electroweak sphaleron freeze-out ($T \sim 130\text{ GeV}$) successfully produces the observed baryon asymmetry $\eta_B^{\rm obs} \simeq 8.6 \times 10^{-11}$ for a benchmark coupling $g_{L_\mu - L_\tau} = 3 \times 10^{-4}$.

**Governing MHD regimes**: The viable parameter space is controlled either by Ohmic diffusion (for magnetic Reynolds number $\mathrm{Re}_{\mathrm{M}} < 1$) or a pre-turbulent frozen MHD stage (for $\mathrm{Re}_{\mathrm{M}} > 1$), with turbulent inverse cascades not having sufficient time to develop before electroweak sphalerons freeze out.

**Opposite signs of baryon and lepton asymmetries**: The generated baryon asymmetry has the opposite sign of the induced lepton asymmetry, meaning avoiding an overproduction of $|\eta_B|$ restricts the inflationary Hubble scale to $H_{\mathrm{inf}} < 10^{-7}\text{ GeV}$ for large initial helicities ($\eta_H \sim 10^{-3}$), a constraint significantly tighter than the requirement that gauge fields do not backreact on the inflaton.

**Viable parameter bounds**: For the benchmark gauge coupling $g_{L_\mu - L_\tau} = 3 \times 10^{-4}$, generating the observed baryon abundance requires $H_{\mathrm{inf}} > 3.2 \times 10^{-8}\text{ GeV}$ and an initial helicity-to-entropy ratio $\eta_H < 2.2 \times 10^{-4}$.

A compelling origin is axion inflation, where an axion-like inflaton couples to a gauge field through a Chern–Simons interaction, exponentially amplifying helical gauge modes that source fermion asymmetries through the chiral anomaly. In this work, the authors consider an extension where the amplified field is a gauged $U(1)_{L_\mu - L_\tau}$ (a flavor-dependent lepton symmetry) and charged fermions are assumed heavy during inflation to prevent Schwinger pair production from washing out magnetic helicity. By tracking the magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) dissipation of this helical field in the radiation era and solving the coupled Boltzmann equations for Standard Model charges, they demonstrate that early helicity decay produces a lepton flavor asymmetry that electroweak sphalerons partially convert into the observed baryon asymmetry before the electroweak phase transition. Crucially, they show that this early dissipation sets tighter constraints on the inflationary Hubble scale ($H_{\mathrm{inf}} \lesssim 10^{-7}\text{--}10^{-8}\text{ GeV}$) and initial helicity than standard inflaton backreaction bounds.

papers.title: Active learning at a graduate summer school: feasibility, student response, and the role of instructor training
papers.authors: Nicholas Kamp, Louis Deslauriers, Carlos A. Argüelles, Gonzalo Herrera, William G. Thompson
papers.abstract: Active learning is becoming standard practice in undergraduate STEM instruction in North America and is slowly being adopted in graduate courses. Graduate summer schools, one- to two-week programs in which students from many institutions gather for intensive, specialized instruction in their field, are common in physics; they are taught by researchers chosen for their expertise, and their pedagogy remains almost entirely traditional lecturing. We report a study at a one-week graduate school in neutrino and astroparticle physics attended by 38 students from 8 countries. Six lecturers with limited or no prior experience of teaching with active learning introduced Peer Instruction-style active learning into their lectures after approximately four hours of preparation led by a physics-education specialist. Each of the three main lecture streams was taught traditionally on one day and in the active format on the other. Students were surveyed after each of the first two days and at the end of the week; all six instructors were surveyed as well. In every active lecture, spanning three instructors and three topics, 82-100% of respondents reported that the interactive segments helped them stay engaged and check their understanding, and in every stream the difficulty was rated as better matched on the active day. At the end of the week, 33 of 36 wanted such teaching in future graduate courses, and not one respondent disagreed. All six instructors judged the approach productive and intend to use it again; only two found implementation straightforward. With brief expert-led preparation, lecturers new to active learning implemented it successfully for a heterogeneous audience, and both students and instructors want more. The school was also the first time any of the six instructors implemented structured active learning: a summer school can develop its lecturers as well as its students.

conclusions: **Overwhelming student endorsement**: In active lecture sessions, 82–100% of respondents agreed that interactive segments helped them stay engaged and evaluate their understanding, and 91.7% (33 of 36) expressed a desire for active-learning techniques in future graduate courses, with no students disagreeing.

**Better perceived calibration**: Across all three core lecture streams, the proportion of students rating the difficulty as "about right" was consistently higher on active days compared to traditional lecture days (e.g., rising from 63.2% to 91.7% in neutrino interactions).

**Feasibility with minimal instructor training**: Six early-career researchers with no prior structured active-learning experience successfully deployed peer discussion after roughly 4 hours of expert-led preparation; all six judged the format productive and intend to reuse it, though only two found real-time execution straightforward.

**Facilitation practicalities**: Student and instructor feedback indicated that the main implementation bottlenecks were question clarity, timing, and having reference materials visible on slides during group discussions rather than the conceptual shift itself.
ai.summary: In graduate physics education and specialized summer schools, instruction has traditionally relied almost exclusively on passive lecturing, despite extensive evidence at the undergraduate level that "active learning"—where lecture time is punctuated by structured reasoning and peer discussion—boosts student engagement and comprehension. To test whether this approach is feasible in advanced settings with novice instructors, the authors integrated clicker-free Peer Instruction into a one-week graduate school on neutrino astrophysics (38 international students), preparing six early-career lecturers through a brief four-hour coaching session. The core curriculum rotated between traditional lecturing and active-learning episodes across three technical streams, with outcomes assessed via anonymous daily and end-of-week surveys. The study demonstrates that even minimal instructor training enables successful implementation of interactive segments, resulting in high student engagement, better-perceived pacing, and strong demand for interactive methods in advanced graduate training.

papers.title: Self-interacting dark matter and neutrino masses from MeV-scale lepton-number breaking
papers.authors: Manoranjan Dutta
papers.abstract: We show that a scalar whose vacuum expectation value (vev) breaks lepton number at the MeV scale, generating the light-neutrino masses through the inverse seesaw, can also serve as the light mediator of self-interacting dark matter. Dark matter is a pseudo-Dirac fermion whose mass splitting arises from the same vev and is predicted to be proportional to the self-interaction coupling times the vev. A strong central interaction between the dark states requires this splitting to be sizable. The CP-even mediator decays into neutrinos at a rate fixed by the neutrino masses, independent of its mixing with the Higgs boson. Fixing the coupling by the relic abundance and evaluating exact partial-wave cross sections, the model reproduces the velocity dependence of the self-interaction cross section inferred from dwarf galaxies to clusters along a narrow band, $m_s\simeq1.9~{\rm MeV}\times(m_\chi/{\rm GeV})$, extending up to $m_\chi\simeq12$~GeV with a best fit at $m_\chi\simeq7.6$~GeV and $m_s\simeq15$~MeV, and on a sequence of resonant islands of comparable fit quality at higher masses. The cluster data bound the dark matter mass from above, so that the allowed masses extend from about $3$ to $70$~GeV ($95\%$ confidence level), with correlated mediator masses of $6$-$28$~MeV. Combining constraints from the effective number of neutrino species, SN~1987A and direct detection, we find the lepton-number-breaking scale confined to a window of a few hundred MeV and a strong preference for normal neutrino mass ordering. The allowed parameter space is testable by future measurements of $N_{\rm eff}$, low-threshold direct detection and the neutrino mass ordering.

conclusions: **Central force requires elastic scattering**: Analytical proof demonstrates that any scalar coupling generating a central Yukawa potential is strictly proportional to the pseudo-Dirac mass splitting ($|g^{\rm central}| \simeq \Delta m_\chi / (2 v_\phi)$), ruling out viable inelastic halo scattering in this framework and requiring elastic self-interactions with $\Delta m_\chi \simeq 2 g_{11} v_\phi$.

**Velocity dependence across scales**: Fixing the coupling by the thermal relic abundance, exact partial-wave cross sections reproduce the observed velocity dependence from dwarf galaxies ($\sigma/m_\chi \sim 1\text{--}10\text{ cm}^2/\text{g}$) down to galaxy clusters ($\sim 0.1\text{ cm}^2/\text{g}$) along the band $m_s \simeq 1.9\text{ MeV} \times (m_\chi/\text{GeV})$, with a best fit at dark matter mass $m_\chi \simeq 7.6\text{ GeV}$ and mediator mass $m_s \simeq 15\text{ MeV}$.

**Cluster bounds on dark matter mass**: High-velocity cluster data impose an upper limit on the dark matter mass of $m_\chi \lesssim 70\text{ GeV}$ ($95\%$ CL), with correlated mediator masses restricted to $m_s \approx 6\text{--}28\text{ MeV}$.

**Symmetry-breaking scale and neutrino ordering**: Requiring $m_s \gtrsim 6\text{ MeV}$ from $N_{\rm eff}$, combined with SN 1987A cooling and mediator decay before BBN, confines the lepton-number-breaking scale $v_\phi$ to a window of a few hundred MeV ($129\text{--}338\text{ MeV}$ for the best-fit point) and strongly favors normal neutrino mass ordering over inverted ordering.

However, light scalar mediators generally face severe cosmological tensions between evading direct-detection bounds and decaying before Big Bang Nucleosynthesis without disrupting the cosmic microwave background. In this paper, the author proposes a model where a scalar singlet breaks lepton number at the MeV scale, simultaneously generating light neutrino masses via an inverse seesaw mechanism and acting as the mediator for pseudo-Dirac fermionic dark matter, naturally decaying into neutrinos on millisecond timescales. By fixing the interaction coupling to match the observed thermal relic abundance and solving the Schrödinger equation in partial waves, the author demonstrates that the model successfully reproduces the inferred velocity-dependent scattering cross sections from dwarf galaxies to galaxy clusters while satisfying constraints from Big Bang nucleosynthesis, $N_{\rm eff}$, supernova SN 1987A, and direct detection.

papers.title: Ultra-Heavy Dark Matter Through Exponential Production Mechanism
papers.authors: Disha Bhatia, Ranjeet Kumar, Rahul Srivastava
papers.abstract: Exponential production of dark matter has been introduced recently as one of the alternatives to the widely studied thermal production of dark matter scenarios. This non-thermal production mechanism leads to the exponential growth in the abundance of the dark matter ($\chi$) through its scatterings with the bath particle ($\xi$), viz. $\chi + \xi \to \chi + \chi$. In our framework, we consider a scalar dark matter $\chi$ charged under $Z_3$ symmetry and bath particle $\xi$ to be standard model singlet and determine the maximum mass of the dark matter using the criteria of perturbativity. We find that dark matter has an upper mass around the ballpark of $\mathcal{O}(10^{15})$ GeV for the cases when the bath particle mass is similar to the dark matter mass. The computations are largely performed with minimal model dependence and will hold in any scenario where the renormalizable couplings driving the exponential growth effectively reduce to $\chi^3\xi$ interactions. Thus, in exponential production of dark matter, we have a possibility of an ultra-heavy dark matter with large couplings, making the scenario phenomenologically interesting. Later, we extend the simplified dark matter model to a UV-complete Dirac Type-I seesaw model where the $Z_3$ symmetry is obtained as a residual unbroken subgroup of a global $U(1)_{B-L}$ symmetry, providing a natural connection with the neutrino sector.

conclusions: **GUT-scale upper mass limit**: By requiring tree-level perturbativity ($\lambda_{\rm exp} \le 4\pi$), the authors establish an upper mass limit of $\mathcal{O}(10^{15})\text{ GeV}$ for dark matter when the bath particle mass is comparable to the dark matter mass ($m_\xi \approx m_\chi$), demonstrating that exponential production can support viable relic abundances near the Grand Unification scale.

**Sensitivity to mass hierarchy**: When the thermal bath particle is lighter than the dark matter ($m_\xi < m_\chi$), the scattering cross-section suffers earlier Boltzmann suppression; maintaining the observed relic density ($\Omega_\chi h^2 \approx 0.12$) therefore demands larger couplings, lowering the maximum viable dark matter mass.

**Distinct coupling behavior**: Unlike standard infrared freeze-in where couplings must remain vanishingly small ($\sim 10^{-11}$) regardless of mass, exponential production requires progressively larger couplings for heavier dark matter, opening parameter space for ultra-heavy dark matter with sizable $\mathcal{O}(0.01\text{--}1)$ interactions.

**UV completion with Dirac neutrinos**: The authors show that the discrete $Z_3$ symmetry enforcing stability and the crucial $\xi \chi^3$ interaction can be realized as an unbroken subgroup of a global $U(1)_{B-L}$ symmetry in a Type-I Dirac neutrino seesaw scenario.

Using a simplified model with a scalar dark matter particle protected by a discrete $Z_3$ symmetry, the authors solve the Boltzmann equations to determine the maximum viable dark matter mass allowed by tree-level perturbativity ($\lambda_{\rm exp} \le 4\pi$). They show that this mechanism can produce dark matter as heavy as the Grand Unification scale ($\sim 10^{15}\text{ GeV}$) while accommodating sizable couplings, and they present a UV-complete Type-I Dirac neutrino seesaw model where the $Z_3$ symmetry arises naturally from broken $B-L$ symmetry.

papers.title: DustER: Dust Extinction with Photometric Red Galaxies
papers.authors: Ivan Espinoza-Bustamante, Eli S. Rykoff, Eduardo Rozo, Chun-Hao To, Supranta S. Boruah
papers.abstract: We present DustER, a new method for reconstructing dust reddening maps from photometric galaxy survey data. DustER uses red galaxies as "standard crayons". That is, it relies on the mean color of red-sequence galaxies being independent of their position in the sky. Given the galaxy's redshift, the difference between a galaxy's observed color and its expected color measures the reddening by dust along the galaxy's line of sight. When using photometric galaxy survey data, the method must rely on photometric redshifts, which, combined with selection effects, bias the recovered dust maps. DustER uses a novel approach to characterize and correct for these biases by leveraging the known statistical properties of the distribution of dust around the Milky Way. Testing on simulations, we find that the recovered dust maps are contaminated by large-scale structure. However, when we use the DustER map to deredden and select red-sequence galaxies, we find the resulting two-point function is not contaminated by dust.

conclusions: Statistically unbiased dust recovery: DustER recovers the input Galactic extinction field E with a mean residual bias of only 0.5 mmag and an rms scatter of 6.3 mmag, confirming that calibrating directly on un-dereddened photometry does not introduce catastrophic offsets once statistically debiased.

Robustness against prior assumptions: When tested on simulations reddened with the Planck GNILC dust map while retaining an SFD-based prior, DustER faithfully tracks the true underlying GNILC field rather than reverting to the prior.

Persistent large-scale structure contamination: Reconstructed dust maps exhibit statistically significant cross-correlations with galaxy density (e.g., 2.7-sigma and 2.3-sigma detections with true magnitude-limited samples in the lowest redshift bins), and standard linear template cleaning fails to subtract this imprint.

Benign impact on clustering observables: Despite the residual LSS imprint in the dust map itself, selecting and dereddening red-sequence galaxies using DustER produces angular power spectra C_ell consistent with truth well within full-sky cosmic variance.

The authors develop DustER, an algorithm that calibrates red-sequence colors directly on raw, un-dereddened survey photometry and recovers dust fluctuations through color residuals, combining Wiener filtering with a statistical debiasing step based on the empirical one-point distribution of Galactic dust. Testing on the Cardinal mock catalog (tuned to Dark Energy Survey Year 3 data), they show that DustER reconstructs dust maps with an rms scatter of 6.3 mmag and a negligible mean bias of 0.5 mmag. Although the reconstructed maps suffer from residual large-scale structure (LSS) contamination that simple linear template subtraction fails to remove, galaxy samples dereddened and selected with DustER recover true angular two-point clustering well within cosmic variance.

papers.title: Leveraging Lensing-driven Early Warnings: Joint Detectability of lensed Gravitational Waves and their LSST Optical Counterparts
papers.authors: Sourabh Magare, Anindya, Anupreeta More, Shasvath J. Kapadia
papers.abstract: Gravitational lensing of gravitational waves (GWs) can be leveraged to provide early-warning times of $\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{hours})$ to $\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{days})$ prior to the mergers of binary neutron stars (BNSs) and neutron star-black holes (NSBHs). This capability could, in turn, enable electromagnetic (EM) observatories to capture transient emissions surrounding the time of the merger. In this work, we demonstrate the viability of jointly detecting gravitationally lensed BNS and NSBH mergers via GWs during the O5 observing run, alongside their associated kilonova counterparts using the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST). We simulate a population of lensed BNS and NSBH mergers detectable during O5 and utilize current benchmark forward models to generate the corresponding lensed kilonova light curves. We then assess the detectability of these light curves across LSST bands under various exposure limits. We find that among the detectable lensed mergers in O5, approximately 60\% of the BNS kilonova and 10\% of the NSBH kilonova will be observable within a single LSST exposure, with mostly quads dominating the detectable population. Furthermore, we define a detectability index ($\rm DI$), which determines the EM-detectability in optical of lensed GW-detectable BNS and NSBH mergers. We demonstrate the robustness and generalizability of the $\rm DI$ on our lensed BNS and NSBH population. Our work demonstrates that lensing-driven early warnings will be highly applicable in the near future, enabling the LSST to effectively follow up on BNS and NSBH triggers within GW localization areas during the O5 observing run.

**Low counterpart yield for NSBH mergers**: Only $\sim 30\%$ of GW-detectable NSBH mergers disrupt their neutron star outside the black hole event horizon to produce an EM counterpart, and of those, only $\sim 10\%$ are detectable in a single LSST exposure, making joint lensed NSBH detections substantially rarer than BNS events.

**Automated Detectability Index ($\mathrm{DI}$)**: The authors formulate and validate (via bootstrapping and 5-fold stratified cross-validation) a data-driven detectability metric that maps lensed GW observables directly to the likelihood of an LSST optical counterpart, offering a practical screening tool to prioritize rapid follow-up during O5 alerts.

Detecting the gravitational wave (GW) from an early-arriving image can therefore provide a pre-merger or early-warning alert, giving wide-field optical survey telescopes like the Vera C. Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) time to point and catch the radioactive thermal transient (the kilonova) in real time. Finally, they construct and cross-validate a data-driven Detectability Index ($\mathrm{DI}$) based on lensed GW observables to rapidly screen which GW triggers are most likely to yield an observable optical counterpart.

papers.title: Conformal Holographic Dark Energy and the Neutrino-Mass Tension
papers.authors: Mario A. Rodríguez-Meza, Jorge L. Cervantes-Cota, Tonatiuh Matos
papers.abstract: Recent DESI results suggest a preference for evolving dark energy (DE) over a cosmological constant, motivating the exploration of alternative models for the background expansion. These data also lead to neutrino-mass constraints close to the lower bounds permitted by oscillation experiments. In this work, we propose and test a conformal holographic dark energy (CHDE) model in which the DE density depends on a power law of the conformal time, characterized by an exponent $n$. The model introduces one additional parameter relative to $\Lambda$CDM and reduces to it in the limit $n=0$. We confront CHDE with BAO, CMB, and SNe Ia datasets, following the combinations used by DESI, and perform parameter inference in both flat and non-flat cosmologies. We find a consistent preference for $n\simeq -0.25$ to $-0.32$, with uncertainties below $\pm 0.1$, and disfavor the $\Lambda$CDM limit at the $4.4$--$4.5\sigma$ level; however, the model-comparison statistics provide no consistent preference for CHDE over $\Lambda$CDM. The resulting neutrino-mass constraints remain compatible with terrestrial limits and yield posterior distributions that peak at positive values, avoiding the negative-mass preference found in $\Lambda$CDM. The CHDE model is therefore consistent with current observational constraints and provides a viable alternative to constant dark energy.

papers.title: Beyond Self-Similarity: Reconciling X-Ray Scaling Relations in Galaxy Clusters and Groups
papers.authors: S. Ettori (INAF-OAS Bologna)
papers.abstract: Scaling relations hold among observed quantities that describe the thermodynamic properties of the gas in galaxy clusters and groups. However, observed data show systematic departures from the self-similar model's baseline predictions, particularly in lower-mass systems. I show that the observed departures from self-similar predictions can be efficiently described by two physical quantities modeled with power laws: the gas mass fraction $f_g$ and the temperature variation $f_T$. Using a wide range of published X-ray scaling relations, this study conducts an MCMC-based meta-analysis to constrain the temperature- and redshift-dependence of the meta-parameters $f_g$ and $f_T$ and calibrate the model. These calibrations indicate that, while the gas mass fraction does not show significant evolution with cosmic time, it decreases significantly with decreasing halo mass. On the other hand, the temperature variation shows a mild positive increase with both mass and redshift. Overall, modeling the departures from the self-similar model with $\{f_g, f_T\}$ drastically improves predictive accuracy, reducing the number of scaling relations in $>3\sigma$ ($>5 \sigma$) tension from 49 (36) percent under the self-similar scenario to just 11 (3) percent (four and one out of 39, respectively) that might be identified for their peculiarity. Moreover, modeling through this generalized framework allows for an extended discussion of the expected slopes and redshift evolution for several X-ray scaling laws, including the new quantity $Y_{LGT0} = L^{-1} M_g^2 T^{a_L}$, a proxy for the cluster's volume that is independent of $f_g$ and $f_T$ by construction, and is predicted to scale directly with mass with a well-defined redshift evolution ($M \sim Y_{LGT0} f_g^0 f_T^0 E_z^2$), as validated against hydrodynamical simulations and observational constraints.

papers.title: Compressed Gaussian likelihood for the Planck low-$\ell$ data
papers.authors: Nanoom Lee
papers.abstract: We present a compressed Gaussian likelihood for the Planck CMB low-$\ell$ E-mode polarization data, constructed from the SRoll2 likelihood which provides the tightest constraint on the reionization optical depth $\tau$ to date. The non-Gaussian form of CMB low-$\ell$ TT and EE likelihoods makes them incompatible with Fisher matrix analyses that require an analytic Gaussian $\chi^2$, such as the Fisher-bias formalism and Fisher forecasts. We show that the $\chi^2$ of an offset log-normal likelihood takes a Gaussian form in the log-transformed power spectrum amplitudes, and can therefore serve as a proxy for the true Gaussian likelihood of this variable in Fisher matrix analyses, without any explicit change of variables. Building on this, we compress the SRoll2 likelihood into a small number of piecewise offset log-normal functions and validate it against the full SRoll2 likelihood via MCMC combined with Planck and ACT DR6 data, finding excellent agreement across all $\Lambda$CDM parameters and in extended cosmological models. We further demonstrate that Fisher matrix uncertainty estimates from our compressed likelihood agree well with the full MCMC posteriors. We release our compressed likelihood planck-gaussian-lowl, a lightweight Python package incorporating the compressed low-$\ell$ TT likelihood from previous work, allowing a straightforward incorporation of the Planck CMB low-$\ell$ data into any Gaussian-likelihood-based analysis. The package is publicly available at \href{ this https URL }{ this http URL }.

papers.title: Calibration of CMB Polarisation Using Cross-Experiment Correlations
papers.authors: Claire Rigouzzo, Eugene Lim, Susanna Azzoni, Yiqi Liu
papers.abstract: Parity-violating physics in the Universe can generate correlations between the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) $E$- and $B$-modes, but detecting such signals requires extremely accurate calibration of instruments. We describe a data-driven method to calibrate the relative polarisation angle between CMB experiments using cross-correlations of observations over a common sky region. Unlike standard self-calibration approaches, this method does not assume vanishing isotropic cosmic birefringence or primordial $EB$ correlations when estimating the relative misalignment angle, and therefore preserves sensitivity to parity-violating physics. As a proof of concept, we forecast the performance of this method using the Simons Observatory (SO) Small Aperture Telescopes (SATs) as a calibrated reference. If they can be calibrated to an uncertainty of $0.08^\circ$, as anticipated from the SO wire grid calibration system, we show that the SO Large Aperture Telescope and Planck could be calibrated to uncertainties of $0.10^\circ$ and $0.17^\circ$, respectively, at $\sim 145$ GHz. This approach relies on the availability of at least one well-calibrated instrument, and provides a complementary path to improving polarisation calibration across experiments, enabling more robust searches for parity-violating physics in the CMB, such as cosmic birefringence.

papers.title: Impact of lensing magnification on the power spectrum turnover
papers.authors: Yolanda Dube, Roy Maartens, Bikash R. Dinda, Sêcloka L. Guedezounme, Sheean Jolicoeur
papers.abstract: The turnover scale $k_0$ of the matter power spectrum -- and consequently of the standard galaxy power spectrum monopole -- encodes a fundamental signature of matter-radiation equality and constitutes an important standard ruler independent of baryon acoustic oscillations. In principle, we can detect the turnover at multiple redshifts and amplify the signal by stacking redshift bins. However, in spectroscopic surveys reaching high redshifts, such as the Euclid H$\alpha$ survey and the proposed MegaMapper Lyman-break galaxy survey, the monopole of the observed galaxy power spectrum receives a scale-dependent correction from lensing magnification. This can modify the signal shape and shift the turnover scale, undermining its use as a standard ruler. Using mock surveys similar to Euclid and MegaMapper, we forecast this shift and the consequent bias in the turnover scale that is recovered from the mock data. The shift in the turnover scale grows with redshift, leading to a maximum bias of $\sim 0.4\sigma$ (Euclid-like) and $\sim 3.6\sigma$ (MegaMapper-like). To avoid a bias $>1\sigma$, the maximum redshift for a MegaMapper-like survey is $z\approx 2.9$. Data in the remaining range $2.9\lesssim z\le 5$ does not directly provide a reliable recovery of the intrinsic turnover. In fact, we find that the turnover vanishes in a MegaMapper-like survey for $z\gtrsim 3.7$. Our results show that the lensing correction to the monopole should be included and carefully modelled when surveys are used to measure the cosmological turnover at high redshifts.

papers.title: Cosmological evolution with decaying dark matter: an integral-equation approach
papers.authors: Nanoom Lee, Anna Bencke, Marc Kamionkowski, José Luis Bernal
papers.abstract: We present CLASSIER-DDM, an extension of the Boltzmann solver CLASSIER that implements the decaying dark matter (DDM) model via its integral-equation approach. The code handles generic two-body decays of a dark matter particle into two lighter decay products with arbitrary masses, naturally encompassing both massless (dark radiation) and massive (warm) decay products, with their perturbations evaluated via integral equations solved iteratively. We describe the numerical implementation in detail, including the background evolution, the iterative perturbation evolution, and a small-scale analytic approximation. A modest number of iterations is sufficient to achieve sub-$0.1\%$ convergence in the matter power spectrum and the CMB lensing power spectrum across the observationally relevant parameter space. We find that a hundred momentum bins for the decay product perturbations are sufficient to achieve $\mathcal{O}(0.1\%)$ accuracy in the matter power spectrum today up to $k \sim 3\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$. The code achieves $\mathcal{O}(1\,{\rm min})$ runtimes per evaluation, requiring neither a Boltzmann hierarchy nor any fluid approximation, making parameter estimation with the DDM model numerically tractable. We also discuss the impact of DDM on cosmological observables, focusing on the case of two massive decay products. This work further establishes the integral-equation approach as a versatile and efficient framework for modeling non-cold relics in cosmological perturbation theory.

papers.title: Cosmological constraints on single-field inflation models from ACT/SPT data and observations at sub-Mpc scales
papers.authors: Qing-Yang Wang, Jing-Zhi Zhou, Fei-Yu Chen, Zhi-Chao Li
papers.abstract: We investigate single-field inflation models that can produce large curvature perturbations at sub-Mpc scales while remaining consistent with cosmological observations across multiple regimes. We highlight the tension between generating enhanced small-scale perturbations and maintaining agreement with the scalar spectral index $n_s$ measured by ACT and SPT, which disfavors several conventional single-field inflation models. To address this issue, we propose three viable classes of inflationary potentials: bump/dip-modified, step-like, and double-inflection-point. Each can sufficiently amplify primordial perturbations while predicting $n_s$ that lie within the $2\sigma$ range of current observational bounds. In addition, we examine the primordial power spectra predicted by these models and constrain their parameter spaces using cosmological observations at different scales, including CMB, BAO, PBH, PTA, and CMB-distortion. Our results show that some of the models considered can simultaneously satisfy the ACT/SPT constraints and account for the current PTA observations, although doing so while respecting the constraints on the PBH abundance remains challenging.

papers.title: A self-supervised machine learning approach to identify instrumental systematics in 21cm Cosmology
papers.authors: Ajith Sampath
papers.abstract: The primordial sound waves in the baryon-photon plasma are imprinted on the large-scale galaxy distribution as Baryon Acoustic Oscillations (BAO), serving as a cosmological standard ruler to constrain dark energy and the Hubble parameter. The upcoming 21cm intensity-mapping arrays are designed to map the 21cm emission across large volumes and measure the BAO scale. However, radio interferometers suffer from instrumental systematics that can hinder detection of the cosmological 21cm signal by leaking bright foregrounds into the signal-dominated modes. This work aims to demonstrate that a self-supervised model can predict the instrument systematic state (here, the amplitude of a spectral ripple in the beam width) in interferometric visibilities and potentially disentangle the instrument from the sky without a forward model. Based on the fact that an instrument stays the same as the sky rotates in a drift-scan observation, and that the same sky is observed under different instrument states, we train a convolutional autoencoder to compress the information in the simulated visibilities and separate this information into instrument-only and sky-only latent vectors. The result shows excellent prediction of the unknown instrument systematic for 15 held-out instrument states with $R^2 = 0.9975$ with a linear probe, against $R^2 = -3.55$ for a random-encoder baseline. The instrument-latent carries no detectable sky signal, as measured with a total-power sky proxy, for any held-out test data. The sky-latent vector and instrument-latent vector show partial separation but not complete disentanglement, identifying sky-latent purity as the primary open problem. The results show the ability of the model to recognize the systematic and show a promising path towards an ML-based foreground cleaning pipeline. Full instrument-sky disentanglement constitutes the natural next step.

papers.title: Short-term optical monitoring of quadruply imaged quasars
papers.authors: L. J. Goicoechea, V. N. Shalyapin, A. Esteban-Gutiérrez, R. Gil-Merino, M. Serra-Ricart
papers.abstract: We present two case studies to demonstrate that short-term optical monitoring campaigns of quadruply imaged quasars (quads) reveal their astrophysical potential. Using the Liverpool Telescope and the third facility of the Two-meter Twin Telescope (TTT3), we monitored the quads QSO 2237+0305 and PS J0147+4630 in the gr bands between July 2025 and January 2026. For QSO 2237+0305, the resulting light curves revealed microlensing variability over a timescale of ~150 days. The g-band difference light curve between images A and B was then used to reliably constrain the half-light radius of the g-band source within the 3.5-16 lt-day range (1{\sigma} confidence level). For PS J0147+4630, we derived new constraints on the AB and AC time delays from the r-band light curves of the ABC images in an arc-like configuration, obtaining 2{\sigma} uncertainties of ~2 days. These constraints were used to shed light on the lensing mass distribution. Overall, our results validate the design of short-term optical monitoring campaigns of quads as valuable astrophysical tools in the era of large-scale surveys. The proof of concept relies on observations with ground-based 2mclass telescopes that lack sophisticated systems to correct for optical distortions caused by atmospheric turbulence, and we indicate the astro-photometric properties of the targets and the monitoring strategies needed to achieve success with these telescopes. Additionally, this work represents the first validation of the TTT3 facility for precision photometric monitoring of gravitationally lensed quasars.
